headline: 126 snakebites and waterborne disease outbreak grip flood-hit Chattogram
summary: Receding floodwaters have left behind contaminated tube wells and damaged sanitation, sparking fears of a secondary health disaster in southern districts.
details: An outbreak of waterborne diseases and a surge in snakebite cases have gripped flood-hit districts in the Chattogram division. Receding waters have left behind damaged sanitation systems and an acute shortage of safe drinking water.
Hospitals in Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, and the hill districts of Bandarban, Rangamati, and Khagrachhari are reporting growing numbers of patients with diarrhoea, skin infections, and snakebites.
The floods, which began on July 8, claimed 23 lives by drowning. Public health experts now warn of a secondary disaster if the drinking water crisis is not addressed quickly.
In Satkania, over 300 outpatient visits were reported in 48 hours, mostly for diarrhoea. In Banshkhali, 30 percent of patients are suffering from diarrhoea, and 15 community clinics were destroyed.
Officials report that around 20,000 shallow tube wells across the division have been contaminated. The Department of Public Health Engineering has distributed 400,000 water purification tablets.
Snakebites have emerged as a major concern, with 126 cases reported across five districts. Boalkhali recorded 26 cases, followed by Banshkhali with 19 and Patiya with 18.
The government has deployed 516 medical teams, including mobile units, across the affected districts. Civil Surgeon Dr Jahangir Alam confirmed that 1,100 vials of anti-venom have been distributed.
Medical experts urge residents to drink only boiled or purified water and maintain strict hand hygiene. Particular care is advised for children, elderly people, and pregnant women.
caption:
126 snakebites and thousands of diarrhoea cases as floodwaters recede in Chattogram. A secondary health crisis is unfolding.

An outbreak of waterborne diseases and a surge in snakebite cases have gripped flood-hit districts in the Chattogram division. Receding waters have left behind damaged sanitation systems and an acute shortage of safe drinking water.

Hospitals in Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, and the hill districts of Bandarban, Rangamati, and Khagrachhari are reporting growing numbers of patients with diarrhoea, skin infections, and snakebites.

The floods, which began on July 8, claimed 23 lives by drowning. Public health experts now warn of a secondary disaster if the drinking water crisis is not addressed quickly.

In Satkania, over 300 outpatient visits were reported in 48 hours, mostly for diarrhoea. In Banshkhali, 30 percent of patients are suffering from diarrhoea, and 15 community clinics were destroyed.

Officials report that around 20,000 shallow tube wells across the division have been contaminated. The Department of Public Health Engineering has distributed 400,000 water purification tablets.

Snakebites have emerged as a major concern, with 126 cases reported across five districts. Boalkhali recorded 26 cases, followed by Banshkhali with 19 and Patiya with 18.

The government has deployed 516 medical teams, including mobile units, across the affected districts. Civil Surgeon Dr Jahangir Alam confirmed that 1,100 vials of anti-venom have been distributed.

Medical experts urge residents to drink only boiled or purified water and maintain strict hand hygiene. Particular care is advised for children, elderly people, and pregnant women.
